p: Thank you for being under two minutes.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and members of the Committee. My name is Kaveh Safehouy. I’m the Executive Director of Lismeth Center for Adult. A founder of literacy partners and a proud member of the New York Coalition for Adult Literacy. As the Council continues to focus on literacy reform, I want to emphasize that New York City’s literacy crisis is a two generational one. The focus on children is critically important and necessary but

if we want to truly address literacy gaps across the city, we also have to invest in the parents and caregivers raising those children. Right now more than 2.2 million adults in New York City have limited English proficiency or don’t have a high school diploma and only two to three percent of those families are being served right now. That’s why we are joining and calling for the Mamdani Administration to invest $20 million in a new city adult education funding stream. Education for integration and equity that Ira spoke about and you had mentioned previously. Uhm and I just want to share a quick story that one of our students in our class has asked to share. When adults build their literacy, English Language and advocacy skills, the benefits don’t stop with them. Those skills strengthen their families, improve child outcomes, and help build healthier more connected communities. I want to highlight two generational impacts with a story of one of our students Yusnia(SP?) who asked us to share her experience in spaces where decisions are made that affect families like hers.

Yusina was detained in a routine immigration status appointment and separated from her husband and child who has autism spectrum disorder for five days. She told us, in the detention center, everything was in English and everyone spoke English. I became the translator for the friends I had made from other countries who were also detained. Helping them communicate their basic needs because they didn’t know how to speak for things in English, even sometimes as simple as water. With a little English I learned in these classes, I was able to help them get the necessities they needed. That experience gave me the confidence to speak without fear, not only to advocate for myself but also for others who had no way to communicate. That confidence and those skills were built in part in the free parent focus ESL classes and she felt English was one of the determining factors that allowed for her release. Yusnia's story is a reminder that we invest in adult literacy. We’re also investing in children, in family stability -
Ten seconds.
In the strength of our communities. Thanks for your attention. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and members of the Committee. My name is Sophia Shi and I am a Program Coordinator here - uh, sorry, at Korean Community Services of Metropolitan New York Inc., KCS. As a nonprofit organization, it has been providing a multitude of services to underserved communities across New York City for over 53 years. In addition KCS is also a proud member of the - of NYCCAL. At KCS, we have seen first hand the importance and positive impact of adult literacy classes in our community. Recently, I spoke of a student who had been attending our ESL classes for over a year. Her initial goals were to improve her vocabulary and grow more confident in speaking with her community members. She is now pursuing a career in translation with hopes to travel around the country. We’ve continuously seen students go above and beyond during initial close, whether it’s in their careers, education or personal aspirations. Our adult literacy services have expanded over the years

to meet increasing demand, however, like others, our resources are limited. NYCCAL is calling on the City Council to increase Council discretionary funding for adult literacy education from $14.5 million to $18 million and to consolidate to two current Council discretionary initiatives for adult literacy and - under adult literacy forward. Our City Council discretionary adult literacy funding is indispensable for over 60 programs and their communities across New York City. As the demand for adult literacy rises, current funding leaves thousands of New Yorkers in need. An additional $3.5 million in funding would help these programs reach the gap. It is crucial to demonstrate to our community members that their interests have not been ignored by increasing funding for these essential programs. Thank you for your attention and consideration.
Thank you.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and members of the Committee. My name is Teresa Alk and I’m the Director of Education at KCS. As my colleagues here have just mentioned, KCS is a proud member of NYCCAL.

For over 20 years, KCS has provided adult literacy classes through city funding. Each year, the steady increase in both our student body and the number of classes offered stands as a testament to the success of our ESOL program and the ongoing need for adult literacy services in our communities. To best accommodate our students' busy schedules, we operate in person and virtual classes Monday through Saturday with flexible morning, afternoon, and evening classes. The impact of these classes can not be overstated. Our students are driven by a desire to engage deeply with their communities and neighborhoods, communicate effectively with family members, advocate for their children, particularly within the education system, ensuring they can stand up for their rights as parents, foster independence, reducing their reliance on others for daily tasks, give back the volunteering and civic participation. Your continuous support has been the catalyst for these transformations allowing our students to lead truly empowered lives. And as everyone has mentioned, we are asking for the similar increases for NYCCAL. City Council, discretionary, adult literacy funding is vital not only to KCS and the

communities we serve but to over 60 programs across New York City, consolidating all City Council Adult Literacy funding and programs under Adult Literacy Forward would streamline the system. I have seen first hand the transformative impact of adult literacy education on our communities. It is time to show our students we have their backs, not just with words but with a necessary increase in funding. Thank you for your attention.
Thank you. I don’t have any questions for this panel. Thank you for your time. Next panel please.
Gerald Kimbrough, Eddie Van, Gregory Ellis, Jeanette Bokanegra(SP?), Alex Griffeth(SP?), Messiah Ramkissoon.
You could start.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens. My name is Messiah Ramkissoon and I serve as a Deputy Executive Director of Youth Justice Network, formerly known as Friends of Allen Academy. Our citywide youth advocacy model serves as the bridge between young people returning home to marginalized communities within the five boroughs of

New York City and their respective needs to support healthier lives and sustainable pathways. The thesis of my message focuses on the importance of accessibility as it relates to intervention and resources and the needed investment to support such infrastructure within the neighborhoods our young people call home. Our work at Youth Justice Network prioritizes proximity and tangibility as two critical components to eradicate cycles of recidivism but most importantly providing doorways to opportunities that can empower healthier outcomes. In 2016, we created a system of aftercare called the Youth Reentry Network, which was catalyzed by our youth advocacy model. This network ensured that every young person entering the doors with new admissions within Rikers was attached to a youth advocate from the first day of incarceration to the day of release, inclusive of but not limited to outcomes around housing and employment, education and mental health. The youth plans created with young people and their advocates during detention were actualized immediately upon discharge. We learned

that young people are more responsive to a model built on trust, rather than one built on mandate. In partnership with the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice and the Department of Corrections, we implemented this initiative within four facilities on Rikers where teams and young adults of all genders were housed. Our services also followed our adolescents who were transferred to ACS custody post Raise the Age. However, due to an unexpected yet impactful COVID budget cuts, we were coerced into a 70 percent layover of staff. I must also add that due to the pandemic, the jail shut their doors to all service providers removing this lifeline of support from our young people. We knew this was the worst time for youth coming from inequitable conditions in communities to be disconnected from the urgent support systems that ensure their wellness. This is when we created shifting gears -
Ten seconds.

A mobile resource center which strives into a different borough each day of the week. We’ve seen an impact with this bus with over 65 percent enrollment in all five boroughs and

young people having accessibility with the resources meeting them on the blocks of the neighborhood.
Thank you.

Thank you. GREGORY Ellis: Good afternoon Council. My name is Gregory Ellis. I’m a Youth Development Coordinator for Youth Represent and today, I was asked to speak here. And my biggest thing was asking myself if we’re serious about this work. How do we keep our young people safe and reduce gun violence in these neighborhoods? I’ve been doing this work for over ten years now and I run across a lot of programs that are not being funded, such as Youth Represent. We are not being funded by the city and we advocate for bills. We are also trying to help these youth with SEL, which is Social Emotional Learning and we do programs every night with these youth. We give them a safe place to stay and talk and have their fun there but at the same time, these nonprofits in our organizations is not being funded by the city. So, we are asking to be funded by the city. Thank you.
Thank you. Thank you for being under two minutes.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and essential members of the Committee on CHildren and Youth. My name is Gerald Kimbrough, I’m an Associate Director of Community Safety at Bronx Community Justice Center, which is part of the Center for Justice Innovation. The Bronx Community Justice Center is one of the center's 35 project sites and serves as a hub for the public safety youth opportunities and neighborhood investment in the South Bronx. Through violence prevention, youth development and workforce initiatives, we tackle - excuse me, we tackle root causes of violence while expanding opportunities for young people and their families. We are asking for an investment to help scale our programming, so that the Bronx can have a fully scaled community justice center. Further, the center also operates Save our Streets, which is SOS. The crime management system in the South Bronx, Crown Heights, and Bedford Stuvessant. Also, through the Rise program, we also address the intimate partnership in violence and gun

violence by helping young people build healthy relationships and solutions. Uhm, thank you.
Thank you. Look at this panel. Appreciate it.

Alright, thank you. Thank you Speaker Menin. Chair Stevens and members of the Committee on Children and Youth for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Alex Griffith and I’m the Senior Director of Programs in core partnerships at Exalt Youth. Exalt serves our court involved youth ages 15-19 year around. Many of the young people that we work with are chronically disengaged from school, over aged and unaccredited. And in some cases, reading at the fourth grade reading level. These are young people who too often have been written off. At Exalt, we take a different approach through a model that combines skill building classes, paid internships earning $18 to $20 an hour, and a strong alumni network. We help young people build the skills, confidence and the real world experience they need to move forward in life. And the results are clear Committee. 95 percent of Exalt alumni do not recidivate. 98 percent are on

track to graduate by the age of 20 and 100 percent of our graduates leave Exalt more employable and ready for the world of work. These outcomes represent real savings and for our city and state. The estimated annual cost to incarcerate a young person as we know, 266,000 to as high as 892,000 per year. By comparison, Exalt’s model is 18 to 60 times as expensive. While producing far better outcomes for young people in our communities. Exalt is also a proud member of the ATI Coalition in the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice ATI portfolio. Alongside our partners across the city, we are urging the Administration to restore and expand funding for ATI and reentry services at MOCJ by $24.6 million above the preliminary budget. The ATI and Reentry Coalition is also requesting an additional $2.4 million from the City Council to support uh, these initiatives. Finally, Exalt is happy to serve as a resource to the Council and city agencies as we work together to expand opportunity to young people across New York City. Thank you for your leadership and your commitment to young people in New York City.

Thank you. I was giggling because uhm, I used to work with Gerald Kimbrough for a lot of lot of years and he called me Chair Stevens. So, now I want to address him as Chair Stevens moving forward. I wanted to say that for the record but thank you guys for being here today and I appreciate all the work that you are doing. Thank you.
Thank you.
For the next panel, we’re going to call Amanda McCarthy, Yessenia Serra, Derek Carter, Lakeraj Gangadin, and Rebeca Chennalier.
You can get started.

Good afternoon, my name is Yessenia Serra and I’m the Adult Literacy Intake and Data Coordinator at Make the Road New York. Make the Road is the largest grassroots immigrant organization in the state serving 30,000 immigrant and working class New Yorkers a year. The majority of them are in New York City. Based at our centers, in Queens, Brooklyn and Staten Island, we support New Yorkers to resolve immigration legal issues by landlord harassment when back stolen wages, access healthcare, improve their English, express themselves through youth arts programs and more.

Thank you Chair Stevens and the City Council for your support of our legal health adult education and art services and thank you to DYCD for partnering with us. Make the Road’s English and civics classes support adult immigrants to navigate everyday life and achieve their goals by obtaining better jobs, gaining work authorization and citizenship. Enforcing workplace rights and helping their children in school, these New Yorkers need the city’s support more than ever, especially given the federal administration's attacks and the dramatic cuts it has threatened to funding that the city relies on for adult literacy. We request that the Council renew $449,637 for Make the Road Under the Adult Literacy Forward initiative to expand the initiative to $18 million and consolidate all Council discretionary funding under Adult Literacy Forward. Funds from Adult Literacy Forward enhance our English and citizenship classes for adults with integrated Know Your Rights education to empower community members to navigate daily life with confidence and security.

This is in addition to NYCCAL’s call for a new $20 million adult ed funding stream, education for integration and equity to expand access. Thank you for your time.
Thank you.

Good afternoon and thank you for giving me the chance to speak. My name is Lakeraj. I am here to share how Forestdale Strong part uhm - Strong Fathers Program changed my life and family. Before I came to Forestdale, I was angry, frustrated and lost. I did not have custody or visitation with my child. I did not know who to turn to. The court and friends recommended the Strong Father’s Program and I joined even though I didn’t want to be there at first. I thought nothing could help my situation. As I engaged with the program, my class facilitator helped me shift how I looked at everything, teaching me to focus on the positives and seeing things from my daughter and her mothers point of view. My father and specialist pushed me to challenge my old ways of thinking and put my child’s need first, not my anger or frustration. One of the

biggest changes for me was learning how to co-parent with another parent that didn’t want to engage. Before I would argue and push, it only made things worse. Once I started listening and responding to my partners concerns instead of reacting out of anger, everything calmed down. My daughter was more at peace. My partner was more at peace, and communication finally improved. My relationship with my daughter is completely different now. At one point, she was calling me uncle instead of dad. It was hurtful but through the program, I learned to understand instead of getting angry, uhm, sorry - over time, our bond grew and today, she calls me dad. That alone tells me how powerful this program is. This is why the program like Strong Fathers and Strong Mothers need continued funding. They help parents who are struggling with real issues, mental health communications and staying connected to their child. I even referred friends to the program because of how much it helped me. There were moments where I wanted to give up but the program stood by my side

supporting me and helped me become the best version of myself. Thank you for listening to me.
Thank you.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and members of the Committee on Children and Youth. My name is Amanda - oh, it’s not on? Oh sorry. Hi my name is Amanda McCarthy. I am the Senior Director and Youth Policy Lead at CASES. At CASES, we believe that too many futures are cut short by unnecessary incarceration. Last year, we served over 12,000 New Yorkers including 741 young people. Our programs prevent young people from experiencing the trauma of incarceration and support their personal goals for education, employment, health, housing, and promote mental wellbeing through clinical and case management services. Access to community based programs is critical to divert young people from entering or furthering their involvement in the criminal legal system. The Fiscal Year ‘27 budget must support the planned expansion of our ACES program with ACS investing $10.1 million for persistent compassionate outreach and engagement for those most at risk of court involvement or violence.

ACES works to divert young men, especially those that are disconnected from school, community and employment opportunities from the criminal legal system. Through persistent outreach intensive mentorship and meeting participants in material immediate needs, are credible messenger staff build trust in meaningful relationships with participants. With this strong foundation, participants share goals and actively engage in their own development. Uhm, they participate in paid employment services, pursue high school equivalency courses and engage in work readiness. 86 percent of all participants successfully avoid rearrest. Expanding ACES to serve more young people in the Bronx, Central Harlem and Brooklyn comes at a critical time. Funding does not meet demand and more young people are becoming caught up in the criminal justice system and detained in juvenile justice facilities. ACES programs have proven that today’s young people need targeted persistent and compassionate support, not detention or isolation from family or the community. We encourage the Council to invest further into community-based programs that involve youth by doubling the funding for the Council’s Court Involved

Youth Mental Health Initiative. This initiative supports mental health services for 3,000 young people.
Ten seconds.
And uhm, we appreciate the city’s commitment to helping New Yorkers avoid incarceration. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you Chair and members of the Children and Youth Committee for the opportunity to speak today on behalf of Forestdale Incorporated. For more than 172 years, Forestdale has dealt with Queens families during their most challenging moments, ensuring that children grow up safe, supported and surrounded by the people who love them. Today, the message I bring is simple and urgent. Prevention works and wraparound support keeps families together. Across Queens, parents are navigating enormous pressures, economic instability, housing insecurity, trauma, and limited access to mental healthcare. These stressors don’t just drain households, they increase the risk of child welfare involvement.

But when families receive the right support early, crises can be prevented, long before they reach the point of separation. Forestdale Strong Mothers and Strong Fathers programs are two of the most effective prevention tools in our borough. Together they reach nearly 600 parents and up to 1,000 children each year. These programs rebuild attachments, strengthen parenting skills and stabilize families experiencing conflict, domestic violence or emotional distress. The results are powerful. In Fiscal Year ‘24 and ‘25 fathers in our program saw a dramatic increase in engagement and financial support for their children and mothers reported improved emotional stability, safer home environments, and stronger bonds with their infants and toddlers. These are everyday victories that keep children safe at home. Our broader family strengthening services show the same pattern, 95, 97 percent of children in our prevention programs remain safely with their parents. 94 to 95 percent of children in foster care achieve strong willed-beings outcomes. These members tell a clear story. When we invest in prevention and wrap around supports, families stay intact and children thrive.

Parents consistently tell us they want to succeed. They simply need community rounded culturally responsive practical support delivered in their neighborhood schools, shelters, and online. Forestdale is committed to meeting them where they are.
Ten seconds.

To continue this work, we respectfully request the Council continue investment in our parenting program including $200,000 for the discretionary funding that sustains and expands these services. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good afternoon. I’m Rebecca Chennalier, Staff Attorney at the Legal Aid Society. Thank you for the opportunity to speak on behalf of the Community Justice Unit. An essential piece of the Crisis Management System that has worked tirelessly to address the systemic issues of gun violence, gang related harm and public safety in the most underserved communities throughout New York City. The need for sustained and restored funding for CJU is not a financial matter. It is an investment in the future and safety of the city, a

commitment to upholding justice, effective gun violence prevention and an essential step in maintaining the trust and care of the communities we serve. CJU is more than a legal service provider, it’s a vital force in the fight for restorative justice within the Crisis Management System. CJU supports and uplifts marginalized communities by providing crucial legal services to high risk youth, families and community members. CJU’s legal services are foundational to the success of violence interruption and preventative strategies. It provides community members with access to legal resources they need addressing the longstanding barriers to justice that have disproportionately impacted them. As CMS expands to over 40 sites across 31 neighborhoods, the demands for CJU’s legal services grow. The ongoing $1.5 million cut in funding to CJU equals 56 percent reduction of services to the most vulnerable populations of New York City. It’s devastatingly impacted legal services providing and is having a direct adverse impact on our ability to sustain prior service levels. It disrupts essential services, not limited but including our legal

clinics, Know Your Right and community events and sends a message that our most vulnerable communities are not a priority. It undermines the very framework of the crisis management system. Data from the New York City Council data team supports and demonstrates the tangible success of the cure violence model with an 18.1 reduction in shooting in the first year and sustained reduction in subsequent years. Community based organizations within the CMS consistently emphasize CJU’s legal services as indispensable in their work to prevent violence and promote public safety. In closing, restoring the funding to the community justice unit is not just about maintaining a service. It’s about reaffirming our commitment to access legal services -
Thank you.
To the most high risk committee. Thank you.
Thank you to this panel, uh.

For the next panel, I’m going to call Jahad Hayle, Expanded Schools, Caitlyn

Passaretti, Galloway, Joshua Castillo, Trenton Price, May Depierro.

Good afternoon Chair Stevens and Members of the Children and Youth Committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Galloway. I’m here to represent the Ali Forney Center, which is the largest provider of housing and services for LGBTQ runaway and homeless youth in this country. Every day our staff and partner providers across the city meet young people who have nowhere safe to sleep. Many have been rejected by their families, pushing out foster care placements or forced to leave unsafe homes. The runaway and homeless youth system is often the last safety net providing services that keep youth from entering in the adult shelter system and out of street homelessness. Yet the system remains severely underfunded. First, we want to urge the Council to increase the RHY bed rate to accurately reflect the true cost of operating beds. Thank you Chair Stevens for mentioning that earlier. So, providers can be asked to do more with what they have instead of less of

what they have. So, we can provide adequate staffing, food, security and supportive services. Second, we strongly want to support baselining $1.6 million for peer navigators and $1.6 million for housing navigators within the DYCD RHY continuum. Peer navigators provide mentorship and guidance from lived experience, helping young people build the trust to navigate the system and connect to critical services. While housing navigators are essential in helping us secure, maintain stable housing in an increasingly competitive market. Without these rules, youth face greater barriers to moving out of shelter and into permanent homes. Finally, I want to name the growing housing crisis youth are facing. Due to federal cuts, young people under 25 have lost access to housing vouchers and many RHY youth cannot access vouchers like HIVP or City FHEPS through the current system. Without vouchers, youth remain stuck in shelters longer, are being pushed towards the adult shelter system. We truly move youth out of homelessness. We need a system that works. That means funding beds at the true cost, ensuring that we have peer and housing navigators and making sure that youth have access to

vouchers. Thank you so much for my time today and I truly appreciate all the ways that you show up Chair Stevens and the Committee as a whole.

Thank you Chair Stevens and the Committee on Children and Youth for the opportunity to testify here today. My name is Jahad Hayle, I’m Director of External Affairs at Expand Ed Schools. Expand Ed Schools is dedicated to ensuring that all young people in New York City have access to enriching programs that affirm their identities, teach them valuable skills, and spark new possibilities in and out of the school day. We are a youth serving intermediary that supports direct service community based organizations across the five boroughs, cultivating partnerships between schools, and communities to deliver high quality programs. For more than 20 years, we’ve invested City Council funds into the CBOs to provide essential afterschool services, professional development, and support for site directors across the five boroughs. In FY 25 alone, we funded programs in 39 Council Districts, supporting approximately 5,800 students, 731 educators and 96 CBOs. Since our inception, we

have served more than 1.6 million public school students, the vast majority of them young people of color living in low income communities. I would like to thank the Council, this Committee, Chair Stevens, and DYCD for the $4 million investment at the school enrichment last year. We are proud of what we were able to do with this partnership with the Council through $4 million at the School Enrichment Citywide Initiative awarded in FY26. Our subgrants help our program, strengthen staffing, serve more students and boost program quality but to meet this pivotal moment, we need to scale and we request additional funding. Our FY27 request is for $6 million. These additional funds will allow Expand Ed to expand at the school slots through K-12 students, improve program quality, and reach communities with continued gaps. We welcome the chance to partner with each Council Member to identify schools in your districts most in need of support. Thank you again for all you do for children and families across the city. I look forward to continuing this partnership.

Hello, thank you Chair Stevens and the Children and Youth Committee for hosting this hearing. My name is Caitlyn Passaretti. I’m the Senior Policy Associate with the Citizens Committee for Children of New York. My testimony will address the needs of runaway and homeless youth, alternatives to incarceration, afterschool and childcare vouchers. The runaway and homeless youth system needs more support. We’re seeing bed vacancy rates are consistently less than one percent across the city every night. We need the city to increase the rates for providers which have not been updated since at least 2017 to $70,000 per bed. This investment will provide safe, temporary housing per youth who otherwise would be without a stable option. We also urge you to restore and baseline the $1.6 million for the housing specialists. Having a trusted support person to offer advice, resources, and answers for young people experiencing homelessness is invaluable. Thank you for your questions to DYCD on that today. In partnership with the New York City Youth Justice Coalition, we are also calling on the city to

restore and invest in programs with proven results to support young people with justice involvement or at an increased chance of justice involvement. We urge specifically the city to restore the $5 million for the Next Steps program, which supports youth with mentorship and support. Please see my written testimony for all the programs we would like to see restored. CCC urges the city to also release the new COMPASS awards from the 2025 RFP process. These awards will allow providers to adequately plan programming and service provision. Additionally, we urge city leaders to remain committed to the expansion of after school by ensuring that the workforce has the necessary support they need to meet the needs of young people, including enhanced rates and cost escalators. Finally, I want to uplift an urgent need to invest in the City’s Childcare Assistance program. Although Governor Hochul’s Executive Budget includes increased investments for CCAP, including $475 million and a one-time funding for New York City. This funding will be insufficient to eliminate the waitlist currently facing approximately $16,000

children and families. We need to address this as fast as we can to ensure that this waitlist does not continue. Thank you so much for the opportunity to provide testimony. Alright, good afternoon members of the Council and Chair Stevens. My name is Joshua Castillo and I’m the Youth Services Coordinator with Vision Services for the blind and visually impaired. A nonprofit that has served New Yorkers who are blind or have low vision for nearly 100 years. Visions provides rehabilitation services, youth development programs, assisted technology training, and independence building services for thousands of children, adults, and older New Yorkers across the five boroughs and Long Island. I’m here to urge you to increase funding for afterschool and out of school youth services in New York City, specifically for youth who are blind, visually impaired and often living with additional disabilities. As a former employee of the New York City Department of Education, I have seen first hand what happens inside the classroom. Teachers are dedicated, related service providers work tirelessly,

and schools are doing the best they can with the time and resources they have. But the reality is this, the school day is focused on academic standards. A typical school day is assigned to me academic benchmarks. It is not structured to fully address the complex layered needs of students who must simultaneously master academics, adaptive technology or additional mobility, independent living skills, social communication and career readiness. A visually impaired student may need to learn how to navigate public transportation safely. They may need intensive instruction and assistive technology, just to complete homework. They may need structured opportunities to build social confidence in a world that is not often not the sign with them in mind. That’s where an organization like Visions plays a critical role. Through the school and out of school programming, we provide young people with hands-on training and mobility, assistive technology, independent living skills and career exploration. We help students practice the real life skills that allow them to travel independently, prepare meals, manage finances and advocate for accommodations.

Vision rehab services such as assistive technology instruction and independent living skills, must be recognized as essential educational supports. Alright, increased funding for afterschool and out of school services is not a charity. It is a workforce development. It is community safety, it is public health. It is a commitment to ensure that disability does not determine destiny. I respectfully ask this Council to prioritize expanded funding for afterschool and out of school programming and to support policies that ensure Vision -
Ten seconds.
Rehabilitation Services, are fully integrated into the educational supports available to students with visual impairments. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you Chair Stevens and members of the Committee on Children and Youth. I am Trenton Price, Executive Director of the Salvadori Center. At Salvadori, we provide steam education services, that stem plus the A for Arts in Architecture, in our case to schools, afterschool

sites and NYCHA community centers across the five boroughs, focusing on the built environment. We are a partner of Expand Ed, our collaborator across the table. For context last year, Salvadori taught over 12,000 students in 178 different sites. We are grateful to have the support of the Council through multiple CASA and digital inclusion literacy grants, as well as afterschool enrichment and the Speakers initiative at numerous NYCHA sites across the city. As a long time partner of NYCHA for almost two decades, we see first hand the need for robust, out of time - out of school time programming for children and youth. In our programs, young people clamor for the opportunity to build and work together and design challenges that will impact their communities. These real life challenges engage their brains. They foster collaboration and they make connections to career pathways that the students may not have considered. With so many pressing priorities for residents of NYCHA, we know that programming for children and youth can sometimes feel like less of a priority but

to the contrary, investing in pathways for children and youth is one of the most critical things we can do to support our success and the success of future generations. I want to thank the Council for their investment in the futures of our youth and encourage you to continue to deepen that support of out of school time programming for young people in NYCHA and shelters who need it most. Please continue to support Salvadori’s Speaker Initiative Funding request to ensure those out of school time opportunities are available for our most vulnerable children and youth. Moreover, we ask the Council to expand the Digital Inclusion and Literacy Initiative Funding, which has been flat for a number of years despite the growing need from youth in school. Thank you.

Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today. My name is May Depierro and I am a Policy Associate Advocates for Children of New York. We are asking the city to invest $3 million to provide interim transportation for students in foster care, awaiting for bus service to begin.

When a student is placed in foster care, they are already facing countless disruptions, uncertainty and trauma. They should not also have to worry about whether they can stay in the school where their teachers and classmates already know their name or how they will get to that school. The city has a legal obligation to provide transportation to students in foster care, so they can stay at their original school. However, it can take weeks or even months for New York City Public Schools to arrange bus service. The city does offer prepaid rideshare when there is no bus available but only after students have already waited at least ten school days. Even once it’s offered rideshare is not always feasible. As an adult must accompany the student, a task that is often impossible for foster parents with jobs or other children in the home who attend schools in totally different communities. Consequently, many students in foster care miss school or are forced to transfer schools even though it’s not in their best interest to do so. In fact, last school year, 55 percent of students in foster care were chronically absent. Meaning they miss at

least one out of every ten school days and one in five transferred schools at least once during the school year. There are solutions from contracting with car services already operating in New York City that use spotted drivers and don’t require additional chaperones, using ACS vehicles that include escorts but these of course require resources. The city must do more to ensure that students in foster care have uninterrupted access to school at a critical moment in their lives and invest $3 million to provide interim transportation for students in foster care awaiting bus service.
Thank you. I don’t have any questions for this panel. Thank you for your time.
Thank you.
